newsitem.title: Tanzania: African leaders ease sanctions against Burundi.
newsitem.headline: African leaders ease sanctions against Burundi.

text.p: African regional leaders eased sanctions on Burundi on Wednesday and urged its military ruler to disband "regroupment" camps for hundreds of thousands of civilians.
At a summit in Arusha with Burundi's Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya, the leaders expanded the list of items excluded from sanctions imposed on Burundi since July 31 last year.

"The regional summit decided...to expand with immediate effect the easing of sanctions to include all food and food products, all items relating to education, construction materials as well as all types of medicines, agricultural items and inputs in order to alleviate the suffering of the people of Burundi," it said.
Fuel and food for aid agencies were already exempted from sanctions imposed six days after Buyoya seized power in a coup by the Tutsi-dominated army and ousted the Hutu president.
The statement said the leaders called on the government to disband all "regroupment camps" and urged the creation of "a conducive spirit for national reconciliation and negotiations".

More than 200,000 Hutu and Tutsi civilians have been ordered into camps guarded by troops since last year. The army says the camps protect people against rebel attack but aid agencies say they are a disaster in the making because of poor conditions.

"Sanctions have been lifted which concern the ordinary people," said Buyoya, clearly bouyed by being invited to his first summit on sanctions and being welcomed by host Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa as "president" for the first time.
"I think it's a very important step. Our expectations were higher. However I think it is an encouraging signal to go forward with the peace process," added the retired army major.
Regional leaders imposed sanctions on landlocked Burundi, demanding Buyoya return it to constitutional rule and open unconditional talks with Hutu rebels. They have not started.
Buyoya has said he is ready for unconditional talks. Such negotiations are opposed by hardline members of the Tutsi -dominated army and former military ruler Jean-Baptiste Bagaza.

Wednesday's summit urged the government to drop restrictions against the national assembly speaker and the international community to put pressure on Burundi through an arms embargo and the denial of visas to those obstructing the peace process.
"The summit declared its readiness to suspend all sanctions with the exception of the arms embargo once there is a movement in the negotiations," said the leaders, calling for a truce.
The ground for easing sanctions was laid by Mkapa in his opening address. "For us today to focus entirely on reviewing sanctions is to miss the forest for the trees," he said.

"Sanctions were imposed only as a tool for a specific purpose. Sanctions were only intended to open the ears, eyes and minds of all stake-holders in Burundi to avoid the path of mutual annihiliation."

The summit was attended by Mkapa, the prime ministers of Rwanda and Ethiopia, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Zambian President Frederick Chiluba, Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, international mediator on Burundi.
In his latest report, U.N. Special Rapporteur for Human Rights Paulo Pinheiro said in February "there is no sign of the beginnings of a Burundi strategy for peace and reconciliation".
More than 150,000 people have been killed in massacres and fighting between the army and rebels since the killing by soldiers of Burundi's first elected Hutu president in 1993.
